label: Plane Conics
notes: Open the chapter. Conics are the first nontrivial plane curves and a perfect testing ground. The deck follows printed pages 19 through 34 and covers the definition of a conic by a quadratic equation, its matrix and discriminant, the projective classification into a few normal forms, and the rational parametrization that follows once a conic has a point.

label: Quadratic Equations
notes: Define a plane conic as the zero set of a degree-two polynomial in two variables. The general conic has six coefficients, so conics form a five-dimensional projective family. Degenerate cases, where the quadratic factors, give pairs of lines, and we keep careful track of when a conic is irreducible versus reducible.

label: Matrix and Discriminant
notes: Encode a conic by a symmetric three-by-three matrix in homogeneous coordinates. The determinant of this matrix detects degeneracy, and its rank distinguishes the cases. This linear-algebra packaging turns questions about conics into questions about symmetric matrices, where the spectral and congruence theory does the classifying work for us.

label: Projective Classification
notes: Classify conics up to projective change of coordinates. Over an algebraically closed field every smooth conic is projectively equivalent to a single normal form, while over the reals a sign invariant separates ellipse-type from empty conics. The number of distinct types is small, which is exactly why conics are so tractable.

label: Rational Parametrization
notes: Show that a smooth conic with one rational point is rational: lines through that point meet the conic in one further point, giving a one-to-one parametrization by the projective line. This is the conic version of the chord construction and previews how rationality questions dominate the study of higher-degree curves.

label: Recap
notes: Close the chapter. A conic is a quadratic curve packaged by a symmetric matrix, its determinant detects degeneracy, projective classification reduces everything to a few normal forms, and a single point makes a smooth conic rational. These ideas set the pattern for cubics and the group law studied in Chapter 02.
